class="wp-block-paragraph">Every year, the global tech ecosystem turns its eyes toward San Francisco for TechCrunch Disrupt, and one key aspect of the massive tech conference is the Startup Battlefield 200.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Selected from thousands of applications worldwide, Startup Battlefield 200 is a curated cohort made up of 200 of the most promising early-stage startups across all sectors of tech including AI, climate, health, fintech, robotics and, yes, drones. When TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 kicks off from October 13–15, 2026 in San Francisco, a number of drone companies — ranging from drone delivery companies to defense tech companies — will have a strong seat at the table.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Here is a look at the drone-focused and autonomous hardware startups that made the cut for this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt cohort:</p><h3 id="h-dexa-logistics-amp-supply-chain" class="wp-block-heading">Dexa (Logistics & Supply Chain)</h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Based in Dayton, Ohio, Dexa is building delivery drones focused on supporting primarily restaurants and retailers, led by founder and CEO <a href="https://www.thedronegirl.com/2024/09/09/beth-flippo-drone-express/">Beth Flippo</a>. In late 2025, <a href="https://www.thedronegirl.com/2025/09/26/dexa-seed-round/">Dexa raised $15 million in a seed round</a>.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">“Being selected from thousands of companies around the world is a huge moment for Dexa,” Flippo said in a prepared statement. “We have spent years proving that drone delivery can move beyond the idea stage and become a real, scalable part of the delivery ecosystem…We believe the future of delivery is in the air, and we are just getting started.”</p><h3 id="h-rocket-fast-drones-space-amp-defense" class="wp-block-heading">Rocket Fast Drones (Space & Defense)</h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Competing under the Space and Defense track, Rocket Fast Drones is an emerging hardware startup developing defense-focused drone systems. As global interest in rapid and mass-producible tactical drones has accelerated, this startup is yet another example of a drone company targeting defense and security applications.</p><h3 id="h-flox-intelligence-smart-cities-amp-infrastructure" class="wp-block-heading">Flox Intelligence (Smart Cities & Infrastructure)</h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Flox Intelligence is an aerial intelligence and wildlife management drone startup. Fresh off winning the grand prize at <a href="https://www.thedronegirl.com/2025/08/25/drone-startups-in-2025/">GENIUS NY Cohort 9</a> and establishing its global headquarters in Central New York, Flox uses specialized drone data to help infrastructure operators, airports and agricultural managers prevent wildlife conflicts.</p><h3 id="h-modal-motors-inc-space-amp-defense" class="wp-block-heading">Modal Motors, Inc. (Space & Defense)</h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">While not a complete drone platform itself, Modal Motors builds key hardware for the ecosystem by way of its lightweight, high-performance electric motors designed specifically for drones, as well as other defense platforms and robotics.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">The company looks to be especially promising as domestic, non-Chinese component supply chains become essential for compliance.</p><h3 id="h-lola-vision-systems-space-amp-defense" class="wp-block-heading">Lola Vision Systems (Space & Defense)</h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Sensor payloads are the eyes of any autonomous platform, and Lola Vision Systems is building them. The Washington, D.C.-based company develops advanced computer vision and optical sensors designed for defense systems, space applications and drones operating in challenging environments.</p><h2 id="h-what-s-next-for-these-drone-startups" class="wp-block-heading">What’s next for these drone startups?</h2><p class="wp-block-paragraph">This handful of drone startups — alongside the total of 200 participating startups — will exhibit on the Disrupt show floor throughout the three-day conference, held in San Francisco’s Moscone Center. Every year, the global tech ecosystem turns its eyes toward San Francisco for TechCrunch Disrupt, and one key aspect of the massive tech conference is the Startup Battlefield 200.

Selected from thousands of applications worldwide, Startup Battlefield 200 is a curated cohort made up of 200 of the most promising early-stage startups across all sectors of tech including AI, climate, health, fintech, robotics and, yes, drones. When TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 kicks off from October 13–15, 2026 in San Francisco, a number of drone companies — ranging from drone delivery companies to defense tech companies — will have a strong seat at the table.

Here is a look at the drone-focused and autonomous hardware startups that made the cut for this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt cohort:

Dexa (Logistics & Supply Chain)

Based in Dayton, Ohio, Dexa is building delivery drones focused on supporting primarily restaurants and retailers, led by founder and CEO Beth Flippo. In late 2025, Dexa raised $15 million in a seed round.

“Being selected from thousands of companies around the world is a huge moment for Dexa,” Flippo said in a prepared statement. “We have spent years proving that drone delivery can move beyond the idea stage and become a real, scalable part of the delivery ecosystem…We believe the future of delivery is in the air, and we are just getting started.”

Rocket Fast Drones (Space & Defense)

Competing under the Space and Defense track, Rocket Fast Drones is an emerging hardware startup developing defense-focused drone systems. As global interest in rapid and mass-producible tactical drones has accelerated, this startup is yet another example of a drone company targeting defense and security applications.

Flox Intelligence (Smart Cities & Infrastructure)

Flox Intelligence is an aerial intelligence and wildlife management drone startup. Fresh off winning the grand prize at GENIUS NY Cohort 9 and establishing its global headquarters in Central New York, Flox uses specialized drone data to help infrastructure operators, airports and agricultural managers prevent wildlife conflicts.

Modal Motors, Inc. (Space & Defense)

While not a complete drone platform itself, Modal Motors builds key hardware for the ecosystem by way of its lightweight, high-performance electric motors designed specifically for drones, as well as other defense platforms and robotics.

The company looks to be especially promising as domestic, non-Chinese component supply chains become essential for compliance.

Lola Vision Systems (Space & Defense)

Sensor payloads are the eyes of any autonomous platform, and Lola Vision Systems is building them. The Washington, D.C.-based company develops advanced computer vision and optical sensors designed for defense systems, space applications and drones operating in challenging environments.

What’s next for these drone startups?

This handful of drone startups — alongside the total of 200 participating startups — will exhibit on the Disrupt show floor throughout the three-day conference, held in San Francisco’s Moscone Center. From this pool, a select group of top finalists will take the main stage on Day 1 to pitch live in front of tier-one venture capital judges, competing for $100,000 in equity-free prize money and the coveted Disrupt Cup.
